rows.en: The term midrash is found in Scripture, as in "the midrash of the prophet Iddo" (2 Chronicles 13:22), "the midrash of the book of the Kings" (ibid. 24). The act of expounding is designated by the verb darash, as in "thus I expounded and thus my colleagues expounded" (Sanhedrin 9:9).⚠1 The masters of midrash are called darshanim (Pesaḥim 70a); this was when they were marked by their particular quality of being learned in the exposition of Scripture, but their title as sages in general was zekenim, "elders" (Sifre Shelaḥ §115, and in many places in the Talmud). Hillel and Shammai in particular were called by the title zaken, as Shammai the Elder, Hillel the Elder, not because they were advanced in years, nor to distinguish them from other sages who were called by their names, but because the title zaken was a proper designation for sages. As to the standing of the midrash and its force: we have already shown that the later sages ascribed to tradition both the old midrashim and the newly made ones, because they believed that these agreed with the first intention of the Giver of the Torah. If there was a dispute over the exposition of the verses, the great court decided (Sanhedrin 9:3).⚠2 This decision was made in this way: the members of the great court stood for a count and decided by the majority, and this was necessarily according to their own judgment (ibid., Bavli 88b). Therefore they ascribed the halakhic consequences that come out of the midrash to the sage who expounded it. And one who decided between two verses that contradict each other and made a compromise between them was called by the later sages "a builder of the Torah" (Yerushalmi Yoma 3:5). The causes that prompt exposition are the fine points of Scripture, which were called dikdukei soferim, "fine points of the Scribes," with respect to the subject, or dikdukei Torah, "fine points of the Torah," with respect to the object.⚠3 The kinds of midrash, however, are various. There are midrashim that explain the intent of the words of the verse, as "and you shall speak of them" [Deuteronomy 6:7], which is aimed at the commandment of the recitation of the Shema, which is the acceptance of the kingdom of Heaven; "and you shall take for yourselves on the first day" [Leviticus 23:40], that the taking be by hand; and many like these. This way of midrash is the most ancient, for it comes to explain the meaning of the words according to their plain sense. But for all that, not all the midrashim that were expounded in this way are ancient, for some of them were expounded for some particular purpose, as we shall see in the example we brought. For surely the most ancient of the ancients did not expound "and you shall speak of them" as referring to the recitation of the Shema, since the verse speaks of the study of Torah. Without doubt the first Men of the Great Assembly already instituted the commandment of reciting the Shema in order to root in the nation the belief in the unity [of God] and the acceptance of the commandments, and the masters of midrash came at some time and expounded the verse for this purpose. There are midrashim that come from reasoning upon the verses, as: "but if the man has no kinsman" [Numbers 5:8] teaches about one who robs a proselyte (Bava Kamma 109a; Sifre Naso §4), for they found no man of whom it could rightly be said that he has no kinsman except the proselyte. Within this class are the midrashim expounded by the rules, and especially by the kal va-ḥomer and the two contradictory verses. And there are midrashim from hints in the verses, as "when she does any one of all the commandments of the Lord" [Leviticus 4:27]: when she does it in its entirety and not part of it (Shabbat 92a); they took the hint from the word aḥat, "one."{v1_09_15:1} All the midrashim fall under these three kinds of midrash, and all the interpretations made in these ways were called midrash,{v1_09_15:2} that is, midrash Torah (Kiddushin 49b), and it was also called "Torah" alone, without the term midrash (ibid., and Yerushalmi Pesaḥim 6:1 and Mo'ed Katan 3:7). The aim of the midrash was to find the sources of the halakhot and to show how they came out of the written Torah, as we saw with Hillel, who went up to the Land of Israel and expounded, and agreed, and received the halakhah (Yerushalmi Pesaḥim 6:1). And we find that a master of halakhot, from whom the source of some halakhah was hidden, praised⚠4 the master of midrash who expounded and agreed with his tradition (Sifra Vayikra ch. 4 and in many places; Sifre Beha'alotekha §79; Tosefta Zevaḥim ch. 1). And just as they made the midrash agree with the existing halakhah, so too they created new halakhot by a midrash that they expounded in the Torah. The effort to find the sources of the halakhot in Scripture was the cause that they widened the ways of midrash and went to excess with the rules of midrash in great exaggeration. Once the ways of midrash had been widened so much, it could not escape producing new things, for they could not set limits to their words: if they used the widened ways of midrash to found the old halakhot on them, they were necessarily bound to rely on those ways when new consequences came out of them.

rows.en: The midrash of the Torah widened greatly through the efforts of Hillel the Elder from the time he reached the office of nasi, and he founded houses for the Torah. Already while still in Babylonia, and before he sat before Shemaiah and Avtalyon, he was engaged in the midrash of the Torah. His teachers, who were great darshanim, further strengthened the longing within him. Besides this, he saw that the time demanded it. For on the one hand there was a necessity to prove that the teaching of the elders was not a new teaching that they had invented out of their own hearts, as the Sadducees thought, but was founded in Scripture; and on the other hand he was compelled to strive to widen the midrash of the Torah, to the degree that even some of the Pharisees had neglected it, as we saw from the matter of the Benei Bathyra and from Hillel's rebuke of them for their lack of exposition. All these signs, together with the fact that Hillel arranged, counted and established the rules by which the Torah is expounded, are clear marks that at the time of his rise to the office of nasi he set his heart to strengthen the midrash of the Torah, and from then on the midrash too began to widen. Yet we have from him, and also from Shammai, only a few midrashim that are called by their names. But this is no proof that others did not exist, for without doubt many midrashim that we have in our hands, on which the names of their authors are not called, should be ascribed to them, and especially to Hillel. Of Hillel seven midrashim are mentioned, and of Shammai four. The character of Hillel's midrashim shows us that by reasoning he went down to the depth of the Torah's intent, and he explained according to his own judgment{v1_09_15:3} even where he was compelled to contradict the meaning of the words as written;{v1_09_16:1} and if at times he explained the words as written, he did so only when reasoning too required it,{v1_09_16:2} or when he practiced the performance of one of the commandments by doing it according to the words as written.{v1_09_16:3} But this is no proof of the character of his way in the midrash of the Torah; it is only a proof that he was scrupulous in the commandments. But in the midrashim of Shammai we find that all are expounded according to the words as written, even where reasoning does not require it.{v1_09_16:4} From this it follows for us that the new road in the midrash of the Torah that Shemaiah and Avtalyon had paved was the way that Hillel chose for himself to attain the widening of the midrash of the Torah; but for Shammai, by his way, the widening of the midrash was an impossible thing. This difference of opinions, which already in the days of the Benei Bathyra was like the letting out of water [Proverbs 17:14] among the Pharisees, broke out further and became like a spring that grows stronger; and when the disciples of Hillel and Shammai multiplied, the dispute increased, and the Torah became like two Torahs. To the same degree that their opinions differed in midrash, they differed in their halakhot. The halakhot mentioned in their own names are few. Of Hillel we have eight halakhot, and it is not told that any of the sages of his generation disputed any of them. Of Shammai we have five halakhot, and on these too we have found no one disputing. Besides these, five halakhot are mentioned on which there was a dispute between Shammai and Hillel. From the halakhot on which they disputed, and still more from the disputes of their disciples, we see that the way of Hillel in his learning was different from the way of Shammai. And although their words are only few, nevertheless we can judge their ways in learning from the fruit of their teaching, which grew and prospered with their disciples; especially since among the halakhot mentioned in the name of the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel there is no small number that date from the time of Hillel and Shammai themselves. Hillel held in one hand the tradition, and in the other the contemplation of this tradition. He inquired and sought to know the causes that were the reasons for the transmitted halakhot, and how, and when, and where those causes would or would not apply.{v1_09_16:5} So he passed over the ancient halakhot in inquiry, and sifted and refined them; and in every new matter that came to his hand, if he saw that by reasoning it was proper to depart from the ancient halakhah, he did not hesitate and departed. But Shammai did not depart from what was received in any matter; on the contrary, he strove to liken every new matter on which he judged to the ancient halakhah that resembled it, even when the case at hand was not truly like the precedent. Hillel's effort was to distinguish by reasoning between things that appear alike and are not alike; Shammai's effort was to bring near by force things that are far apart, and to liken things that are not alike except to the eye, by his casuistry and sharpness of intellect (Yevamot 13b). Accordingly, both engaged in the criticism of the halakhah, except that with Hillel criticism was the measure for keeping or annulling the halakhah, while with Shammai the halakhah was the measure for criticism and inquiry. If we want to know what the later sages thought of Shammai's character and how they judged him, we must look at their judgment of the man whom the later sages likened to Shammai. This man was R. Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, of whom they said that he was a Shammuti [a follower of Shammai]. They gave him this name not because he was a disciple of Shammai, for he was not, but because he walked in Shammai's footsteps. And from all we know of this R. Eliezer we understand that his way in learning was as we have described Shammai's way. R. Eliezer too did not depart a hair's breadth from what was received, and said nothing that he had not heard from his teachers; and on every new case about which he had not heard what the earlier sages said, he said, "I have not heard," and did not decide by his own opinion (Sukkah 27b). He also treated his rules alike and made no distinctions (Yevamot 108b), and he did not permit his disciples to give a reason for a halakhah except to uphold the ancient halakhah (Nega'im 11:6, and Sifra Tazria ch. 6 and ch. 15); and further matters of this kind are told of him, all of which agree that his ways in learning were along the path we have described. Therefore from the thing compared we can judge the thing it is compared to. Now clinging to what is received, without distinguishing between like and unlike, leads mostly to new stringencies, and the reverse to the reverse. This was borne out in Hillel and Shammai and their disciples: Shammai and his House mostly came out with stringencies, and Hillel and his House the reverse. The most trustworthy proofs, which bear witness how firmly Shammai held to tradition without departing from what was received even in a matter where the case at hand did not resemble the precedent laid down in the ancient halakhah, are revealed and seen from several deeds told of Shammai the Elder. They said of him that he did not want to feed his little son on the Day of Atonement, and the sages decreed against him and made him feed him with his own hand⚠1 (Tosefta Yoma ch. 4).{v1_09_17:1} This was surely because he relied on an ancient halakhah that children are trained in the commandments, and he did not distinguish between one child and another, or between one matter and another. Perhaps it was because of this event that they fixed the halakhah: "Children are not made to fast on the Day of Atonement, but they are trained a year or two before" (Yoma 82a). And another time he showed his strictness in the training of children: his daughter-in-law gave birth to a son on the festival of Sukkot, and he broke away the plaster of the roof and covered it with sukkah branches over the bed for the sake of the child (Sukkah 28a). Such deeds need no explanation, but anyone who has eyes will see how much Shammai refused to depart from the very substance of what was received, even where there was no room for the reason of the received thing. The same is seen from his halakhot. Regarding the impurity of the tent, Shammai held that a quarter[-kav of bones] from a single bone defiles (Eduyot 1:6); here he relied on the halakhah that a quarter causes impurity and did not depart from it in any case, and decided that this quarter applies in all cases, even from a single bone. And so with his saying, "For all women their time suffices" (Niddah 1:1): surely there was a received halakhah that a woman is not presumed impure as a menstruant until she sees [blood], and this is indeed the law of the Torah; therefore he did not depart from it, even though reasoning suggests one should fear that, as she is now found impure, so she had already been impure before this. In this case we see that by his way a leniency came out for him.

1.note: Literally 'and they fed him by his hand'; read with the Tosefta as: they made Shammai feed the child with his own hand (see note 1 on this page).

rows.en: Not so did Hillel. He sifted and refined the ancient halakhah, and distinguished by rational reasoning between one act and another and between one time and another; he examined the reason for the matter, and according to his examination he gave it validity or annulled it. So it appears from his halakhot, and still more from the halakhot that were said and taught in the name of the House of Hillel, as will be made clear. This way of criticism runs also through the enactments that he made. Of his enactments only two have been preserved for us that are ascribed to him with certainty. The first is this: when he saw that the people refrained from lending to one another and transgressed what is written in the Torah, "Beware that there be not a base thought in your heart" etc. [Deuteronomy 15:9], he instituted the prosbul (Shevi'it 10:3). The aim of the prosbul is that the Sabbatical year should not cancel the loan, and by this he uprooted the commandment of the release of debts written in the Torah. The text of the prosbul is: "I hand over to you, So-and-so and So-and-so, the judges in such-and-such a place, that any debt that I have, I may collect it whenever I wish"; and the judges sign, or the witnesses (ibid. 10:4).{v1_09_18:1} From this enactment it appears that his whole aim was to go deep into the intent of the Torah and to reach the end of its purpose. For he recognized that the aim of the statutes of the Torah is to strengthen the moral law, and he saw that the statute of the release of debts came into conflict with another statute, namely, to lend to the poor man in his time of need, and through this the virtue of morality and kindness suffered; and we cannot uphold the one unless we break the other. But according to the demands of his time the one was more needed than the other; therefore Hillel did not hesitate to uproot the one in order to give standing to the one more needed. Another enactment is mentioned in his name, concerning one who sells a house among the houses of walled cities: by the law of the Torah it may be redeemed until a full year has passed, and if the last day of the twelfth month arrived and it was not redeemed, it became the buyer's for good. They used a trick: the buyer would hide on the day the twelve months ended, so that the seller could not redeem it and it would become his for good. Against this Hillel enacted that [the seller] might throw his money into the chamber, and break [the door] and enter, and the buyer would take his money (Arakhin 9:4). Of the rest of his enactments we have not been told. One may also ascribe to Hillel and the men of his time what was enacted: that they prepare for the High Priest on the Day of Atonement another priest in his place, lest some disqualification befall him and he be unable to perform the service (Yoma 1:1). This statute was enacted because of an event that happened when Mattathias ben Theophilus⚠1 was High Priest: a nocturnal emission befell him on the night of the Day of Atonement, and Joseph ben Ellem served in his place; and because of this event it became a statute that every year they would prepare another priest in his place (Yerushalmi Yoma ch. 1, and Tosefta ch. 1; see Graetz vol. 3, p. 30?).⚠2 Now this priest held his office in the time of the presidency of Hillel the Elder (around the year 3756 of Creation), and without doubt the enactment came from him and from his court. There is also no doubt that it was then that they enacted that the priest should stay awake all night and expound the Torah, or that others expound before him, so that he not sleep; and they further enacted that he not eat much on the eve of the Day of Atonement, to guard against a nocturnal emission. For from what happened to Mattathias it appears that until that time it was not the custom that the priest stay awake all night (Yoma 1:4 and 1:6). In all the enactments that Hillel made we do not find that Shammai opposed him, for Shammai too did not shut his eyes to the needs of the time, and he said so explicitly. At that time the tillers of the soil treated the Sabbatical year lightly: not only did they plow their fields in the Sabbatical year, but they did the plowing in the best possible way. This was evil in the eyes of Shammai, and he said of such a field that had been improved in the Sabbatical year: "If the hour were free, I would decree that it not be sown" (Tosefta Shevi'it ch. 3). And what was there in that time, of which Shammai said that it was not fit for decreeing a decree? It seems that the reason was this. It is known how heavy the yoke of taxes was on Israel in the days of Herod, for he took all their labor. And to gain the gain of extortion, his eyes and heart were always on the labor of the people, lest the spring from which he drew his extortion be stopped. Therefore he strove to remove every statute and law that kept the people from working the land — which was their chief occupation. To be sure, he feared to break the statute of the Sabbatical year because of the zeal of the people and the sages; but without doubt there was a royal decree that at least all work for the needs of the year after the Sabbatical year be done in the Sabbatical year. Therefore Shammai's words are aimed at this: that the hour is not free to decree this decree. This matter, that the government forced them to plow in the Sabbatical year, happened at various times, and the sages of the generation always permitted it.{v1_09_19:1}

footnotes.en: I have been precise in saying that the hint is from the word aḥat, and not as the Tosafot on Shabbat (3a),⚠1 who understood that be-asotah is expounded as referring to the labor; this is not so. All the fine points of the Tosafot are only for casuistry, and it is not right that we ascribe to the masters of the Talmud, on account of slight fine points, interpretations that reason and language cannot bear. Know that were it not for the hint in the word aḥat, which indicates the whole of it, since part of one is not fit to be called "one," on the contrary, from be-asotah we could have expounded even part of it. For in Sifre Shelaḥ §110 it expounds "when you come into the land" [Numbers 15:18]: Scripture changed this coming from all other comings, for of all other comings it says "and it shall be when you come" etc., "and it shall be when [the Lord] brings you," but here it says be-voakhem, to teach you that as soon as they entered the land they became liable to ḥallah. The meaning is clear: tavo'u, "you shall come," in the future, refers to a complete coming, that is, after their coming is already complete; but be-voakhem, in the infinitive, refers to part of a coming, that is, as soon as the coming begins. If so, we would likewise expound here: had it been written ve-asetah or ta'aseh, the meaning would be a complete doing, but from be-asotah we could expound even part of a doing. Therefore its exposition is only from the word aḥat.

1.note: The folio letter is faint; read ג (Shabbat 3a, where Tosafot discuss בעשותה). OCR had נ.

footnotes.en: Everything learned by the rules is called midrash, Yerushalmi Kiddushin 1:2 and Bavli (10b),⚠1 whether it is learned by kal va-ḥomer, by gezerah shavah, or by the other rules. It is surprising that we find in Tosefta Sanhedrin ch. 6: "midrash and kal va-ḥomer are subject to midrash," which distinguishes between kal va-ḥomer and midrash. Maimonides, ch. 4, halakhah 8 of [Hilkhot] Talmud Torah, copied the Tosefta, and his reading is: "midrash and aggadah are subject to midrash; aggadah and kal va-ḥomer are subject to kal va-ḥomer; kal va-ḥomer and gezerah shavah are subject to kal va-ḥomer." It seems that there is a difference between midrash and things that come by the rules, against the Talmud.⚠2 But it follows for us from this that they used the word midrash in two senses: the first is midrash in its narrow sense, which is the interpretation of Scripture not by the rules; the second includes every exposition of the verses, in whatever way it may be.

1.note: So printed; the Bavli passage defining midrash is at Kiddushin 49b.

2.note: Reading נגד is from the print; sense: contrary to the Talmud's usage, which calls all such learning midrash.

footnotes.en: Hillel expounded: one verse says "and you shall sacrifice the Passover-offering ... of the flock and the herd" [Deuteronomy 16:2], and another verse says "from the sheep and from the goats you shall take it" [Exodus 12:5]; how so? The flock for the Passover-offering, the flock and the herd for the festival-offering (Yerushalmi Pesaḥim 6:1); and see Mekhilta Bo ch. 4, Bavli ibid. (70b) and Menaḥot (82a). He further expounded: one verse says "six days you shall eat unleavened bread" [Deuteronomy 16:8], and another verse says "seven days" [Exodus 12:15]: six from the new [grain] and seven from the old (Yerushalmi ibid.); and Mekhilta Bo ch. 8, in the name of "another interpretation"; and Sifre Re'eh in the name of R. Simeon; and Menaḥot (66a) in the name of R. Simeon ben Elazar; and see the Tosafot there. In these he decided by his own judgment.

He further expounded: "the scall is healed" [Leviticus 13:37] — and not that a scall broke out within the scall. For by the meaning of the words as written he should be pure, since the scall has healed and the condition of the scall is fulfilled; but he departed from this sense because reasoning requires the opposite, for he understood the Torah's intent to be that every scall disease causes impurity, and he cannot be declared pure unless he is completely healed. He likewise expounded: "the scall is healed, he is pure" — could he then be released and go off? Scripture says, "and the priest shall pronounce him pure" ... could it be that if the priest said of an impure one "pure," [he is pure]? Scripture says "he is pure": he must be pure. In this too he explains that "and the priest shall pronounce him pure" is not to be understood literally, as though impurity and purity were in the hand of the priest; rather impurity depends on the presence of the scall, and purity on its healing, and the priest's task is only to determine whether the scall is present or has healed (see Sifra Tazria ch. 9; Tosefta Nega'im ch. 1). "On the seventh day he shall shave it, and on the eighth day he shall bring two turtle-doves" [Numbers 6:9–10]: if he shaved on the eighth, he brings the offerings on the ninth (Nazir 44b). This is from reasoning: since it is said that the shaving and the bringing of the offerings are to be on two different days, he concluded from this that also when he shaved on the fifth⚠1 he should not bring the offerings according to the meaning of the words as written, that is, on the eighth, but on the day after.

1.note: So printed (ה' = fifth); the sense requires ח', the eighth.

footnotes.en: "Whoever touches their carcass shall be impure" [Leviticus 11:36] — even when they are in the water (Sifra Shemini ch. 9). He expounded the words as written because reasoning requires it, for how can one who immerses in water become pure while a creeping thing is in his hand?

"With unleavened bread and bitter herbs they shall eat it" [Numbers 9:11]: that he wrap them together at once and eat them (Pesaḥim 115a, and in the Tosefta there). Hillel practiced so for himself, and we do not find that Hillel said that this is a fixed statute not to be transgressed; rather he did so as the choicest way of the commandment. This is the meaning of the baraita: "Could it be that he wraps them together as Hillel did, etc." — that is, could it be that what Hillel did is a fixed statute not to be transgressed? But the baraita does not dispute Hillel, nor Hillel the baraita. The masters of the Gemara, however, did not understand it so.

Shammai expounded "until it falls" [Deuteronomy 20:20] — even on the Sabbath (Shabbat 19b; Tosefta Eruvin ch. 3). "You have slain him with the sword of the children of Ammon" [2 Samuel 12:9]: to teach that one who says to his agent, "Go and kill a person," the sender is liable (Kiddushin 43a). Impure leaven or spices do not impart impurity until there is the size of an egg in them (Orlah 2:5); without doubt he learned this from an exposition, as is explained in Sifra Shemini ch. 9: "any food ... shall be impure" [Leviticus 11:34] teaches that it becomes impure in any amount; could it make others impure in any amount? Scripture says "which may be eaten" — thus it does not impart impurity except in the size of an egg. The midrash brought in the name of Elazar ben Ḥananiah ben Ḥizkiah⚠1 ben Gurion: "Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy" [Exodus 20:8] — keep it in mind from the first day of the week, so that if a fine portion comes your way you prepare it for the Sabbath (Mekhilta Yitro ch. 7) — it seems that this midrash was received from Shammai, of whom they said that all his days he ate in honor of the Sabbath: if he found a fine animal, he said, "This is for the Sabbath," etc. (Beitzah 16a). This agrees with what they said in the name of the House of Shammai: "from the first day of the week, for your Sabbath."

The Sabbath basket: Hillel forbade it for himself (Tosefta Ma'aserot ch. 3): one who gathers a basket to send to his fellow may not eat until he tithes; R. Judah said: Hillel forbade it for himself (ibid., and Beitzah 35a). Rashi explains that he alone forbade it, and the sages of his generation disputed him. But on the Sabbath basket the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel also dispute; from this it appears that the incident first happened to Hillel and he forbade it to himself, and his disciples took this stringency as halakhah. Hillel says⚠1 [one may not] say, "Lend me until my son comes," or "until I find the key"; and he likewise used to say: a woman may not lend a loaf to her neighbor until she sets a value on it, lest wheat rise in price and she come to interest (Bava Metzia 75a; and see Tosefta there ch. 6). Hillel handed down the halakhah that the Passover-offering overrides the Sabbath, and that rabbinic Sabbath prohibitions are set aside for the sake of a commandment (Pesaḥim 66a); and that a man may bring his burnt-offering unconsecrated into the Temple court and consecrate it [there] (Nedarim 9a). Shammai says: vetches of terumah are to be eaten dry (Ma'aser Sheni 2:4); a sela of second tithe should not be changed, but one should leave it in the shop and eat against its value (ibid. 2:9); the frame of a chair is impure, and likewise one made inside a kneading trough is impure (Kelim 24:3); a quarter[-kav] from a single bone, of the spine or of the skull, defiles in a tent (Nazir 53a; and see Eduyot 1:6). And these are their disputes: Shammai says not to lay hands, and Hillel says to lay hands (Ḥagigah 2:2); Shammai says, "For all women their time suffices," and Hillel says, "from examination to examination" (Niddah 1:1); Shammai says a kav [is liable] to ḥallah, and Hillel says two kavs (Eduyot 1:2); Hillel says a full hin of drawn water disqualifies the immersion pool, and Shammai says nine kavs (ibid. 1:3); one who gathers grapes for the press — Shammai says they have become susceptible [to impurity], and Hillel says they have not become susceptible (Shabbat 15a; see there). In some of them Shammai is the lenient one; and see what I wrote in the introduction to the Mekhilta with my commentary *Middot Soferim*.

1.note: So printed (אומר); Mishnah Bava Metzia 5:9 has אוסר, 'forbids', which the sense requires.

footnotes.en: In the Bavli, Yoma (77b), the reading is that he did not want to feed him with one hand, and they decreed that he feed him with both hands; and the Gemara explains the reason as being because of Shivta [an evil spirit]. Accordingly the chief objection was that he did not want to wash his hands, and not the training of the child. But in the Tosefta mentioned in the text it is proved plainly that the reason he did not want to feed him was the training of the child; I have followed the Tosefta, and the words of the Gemara need study.

The law of the prosbul applies both to a loan by deed and to an oral loan; except that in the view of the Talmud, for a loan by deed one does not by law need a prosbul, but only hands his deeds to the court, for so we learned: "one who hands his deeds to the court, [the Sabbatical year] does not cancel." And in Gittin (1a):⚠1 "I hand [it] over to you, that you be the exactors and I will not exact." And in Makkot (3a) he [Rashi] explains that handing one's deeds to the court is the prosbul; but the Tosafot there dispute this and write that handing one's deeds to the court and the prosbul are two different things, and so is the view of Maimonides, ch. 9 of Hilkhot Shemittah; and Rashi stands alone in this view. But Rashi's source is from Sifre Re'eh §113: "'what is yours with your brother your hand shall release' [Deuteronomy 15:3] — and not one who hands his deeds to the court; from here they said: Hillel instituted the prosbul." At first sight this is as Rashi's view. But in Yerushalmi Shevi'it 10:3 they said: "From here they found support for the prosbul, that it is from the Torah. Is the prosbul from the Torah? When Hillel instituted it, they supported it with words of Torah." Accordingly, the intent of the Sifre is: since the handing over of deeds is a matter of Torah, Hillel too instituted the prosbul. So the Ran explained, and his proof is from the Mishnah where we learned: "One who lends on a pledge, and one who hands his deeds to the court, [the Sabbatical year] does not cancel; a prosbul, it does not cancel." As for Rashi's explanation, "that you be the exactors and I will not exact," the meaning is not that the court collects the debt, for [the lender] wrote: "whenever I wish I may collect it" — so the court does not collect. And we learned: "A creditor who produces a bond of debt and there is no prosbul with it — these are not paid" (Ketubbot 9:9); so the deed and the prosbul were in the hand of the lender. But Rashi's intent is that through the prosbul he is not counted as an exactor if he collects the debt; rather the exacting comes from the side of the court. I have written all this because I saw that others erred in these laws. Know that this midrash, "what is yours with your brother your hand shall release" etc. — "and not one who hands his deeds to the court," in my opinion was newly made after Hillel's enactment. For Hillel's enactment, to uproot the release of debts, which is a commandment written in the Torah, was hard in their eyes; therefore they strove to find it a support and expounded that for one who hands his deeds to the court [the year] does not cancel by law, and in this way they supported Hillel's enactment on the exposition of the verse. For if the law had already existed, from the meaning of the verse in the Torah, that for one who hands his deeds to the court [the year] does not cancel, it would not have been so necessary to make an enactment to uproot a law of the Torah.

1.note: So printed; the words מוסרני לכם are in Mishnah Shevi'it 10:4, discussed at Gittin 36a–b.
